newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-TNT in talks with ACCC on freight.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-TNT in talks with ACCC on freight.

text.p: Transport group TNT Ltd confirmed on Friday it had been approached by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) over the consumer watchdog's probe of misleading conduct in the freight business.
"The ACCC has been in contact with us and we have had discussions with them and the outcome of those discussions have not been made public," TNT spokesman Mark Gell told Reuters.
Gell declined to comment on the talks, but an industry source told Reuters they focused on the group's TNT Air Crews business, which was to change its name.

The ACCC is investigating claims that freight companies are leading customers to believe that priority parcels for overnight delivery in Australia are being sent by air, when in fact they are delivered by road.

At least one major freight company, Mayne Nickless unit Ipec Priority Express, has admitted to misleading customers after the ACCC revealed it had planted altimeters in parcels and arranged to have them flown between major cities.
"Data retrieved from the alimeter indicated that the parcels never achieved altitudes higher than various points along the Hume Highway (between Melbourne and Sydney), the ACCC said on Thursday.
Ipec Priority Express was one of "various companies" investigated in this way, it added. It did not name the others.

Ipec Priority Express has offered to pay refunds or credits of A$50 each for people who used its service in the year to June, Mayne Nickless spokesman Carl Kitchen said on Friday. He estimated the refunds could cost the company up to A$350,000.
"The ACCC is investigating allegations of similar conduct throughout the industry and expects reform within months," ACCC chairman Allan Fels said in a statement on Thursday.
Asked to elaborate on Friday, an ACCC spokeswoman said, "Watch this space."
Asked if TNT would also be offering refunds to customers, group spokesman Gell declined to comment.
